item.title: Turning Sub-Saharan Africa’s Cities Into Job Engines
item.dc:creator: Paschal Donohoe
item.description: Cities and towns will be central to creating more and better jobs for Sub-Saharan Africa’s fast-growing population, simply because the region’s people and economic activity are increasingly concentrated there. But unlocking urbanization’s potential requires policy guidance and well-planned investment.
item.content:encoded:
Photo: Per-Anders Pettersson/Getty Images

Cities and towns will be central to creating more and better jobs for Sub-Saharan Africa’s fast-growing population, simply because the region’s people and economic activity are increasingly concentrated there. But unlocking urbanization’s potential requires policy guidance and well-planned investment.

By Paschal Donohoe

WASHINGTON, DC—Recent visits to South Africa and Ghana brought home to me the scale of Africa’s urban development opportunity. In Johannesburg and Accra, I saw fast-growing cities, teeming with ambition, innovation, and young people looking to build better lives. Their challenges are significant, but so, too, is their potential to create jobs and drive growth.

item.title: Why Are Indian Protesters Targeting the Electoral Commission?
item.dc:creator: Shashi Tharoor
item.description: Following a “special intensive revision” that struck 130 million voters from the electoral rolls, India’s youth have mounted large-scale protests against the Election Commission. Given the convergence of protests with the formal political opposition, the Commission is unlikely to avoid accountability for mass disenfranchisement.
item.content:encoded:
Photo: Arun Sankar/AFP via Getty Images

Following a “special intensive revision” that struck 130 million voters from the electoral rolls, India’s youth have mounted large-scale protests against the Election Commission. Given the convergence of protests with the formal political opposition, the Commission is unlikely to avoid accountability for mass disenfranchisement.

By Shashi Tharoor

NEW DELHI—Following a summer of discontent, India has entered an autumn of political crisis. During a scorching June and July, a youth-led movement, backed by Rahul Gandhi’s opposition Congress party, took to the streets to demand education reform. So potent was the movement that the central government, led by the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP), was forced to make significant concessions, including the resignation of Union Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan. But Indians are not finished: they have now set their sights on the electoral system.

item.title: Why Aren’t We Investing More in Climate Adaptation?
item.dc:creator: Mekala Krishnan, Sylvain Johansson and Kanmani Chockalingam
item.description: There are many proven ways to protect people and assets from extreme weather, and such measures often prevent economic losses worth many times their cost. But ensuring their implementation requires making them more affordable and creating innovative revenue mechanisms and financing structures.
item.content:encoded:
Photo: Christian Charisius/picture alliance via Getty Images

There are many proven ways to protect people and assets from extreme weather, and such measures often prevent economic losses worth many times their cost. But ensuring their implementation requires making them more affordable and creating innovative revenue mechanisms and financing structures.

By Mekala Krishnan, Sylvain Johansson and Kanmani Chockalingam

BOSTON/GENEVA/SEATTLE—As world leaders gather in Antalya, Turkey, for the United Nations Climate Change Conference (COP31), climate adaptation is high on the agenda. The economic case for action is compelling. Measures ranging from flood defenses to cooling and irrigation technologies can prevent losses—including property damage, lower productivity, and reduced agricultural yields—worth many times their cost. Yet the world invests only a fraction of what’s needed, leaving many people and assets inadequately protected from extreme weather.

The McKinsey Global Institute (MGI) found that the world spends approximately $190 billion annually on 20 proven adaptation measures that protect against heat, wildfire, flooding, and drought. But this is just one-third of the $540 billion needed to protect everyone exposed to climate hazards at developed-economy standards. These measures could cost $1.2 trillion per year when the world reaches 2° Celsius above pre-industrial levels, which current emissions trajectories suggest may occur by around 2050. But we estimate that the returns in avoided losses would be roughly three times the costs of these measures today, increasing to seven times the costs at 2°C of warming.

Clearly, economic benefits are not enough to guarantee investment. The problem is that what makes economic sense for society does not always make financial sense for the households, companies, and governments expected to act. Consider the construction of a sea dike. It protects residents, businesses, property owners, and insurers from flood losses, but the public agency building it has no way to recover its costs, because a sea dike does not produce revenue. Similarly, a bank may struggle to finance an asset with no predictable cash flow.

New research from MGI examining investment barriers across 20 measures finds two preconditions for climate adaptation: households, companies, and governments must be willing and able to implement measures, and capital providers must be willing to finance them on acceptable terms. Competing spending priorities, unclear benefits, misaligned incentives, and implementation challenges can constrain demand, while repayment risks, uncertain project performance, and the difficulty of making numerous small investments can impede financing even where demand exists.

While these barriers often reinforce one another, they are not universal. By 2050, we estimate that measures representing roughly $460 billion in annual adaptation costs—about 40% of the total needed—could be “deployment ready,” facing minimal demand or financing constraints. Beyond protecting lives and livelihoods, these measures, which range from cooling systems to stormwater management, represent a potential market opportunity for adaptation providers and financiers, and over two-thirds of this opportunity is expected to be in higher-income regions.

But substantial obstacles stand in the way of unlocking the remaining $690 billion in annual adaptation costs required at 2°C, particularly in the least protected places. In India and Sub-Saharan Africa, adaptation costs could reach 2–3% of GDP, compared with 0.3–0.5% in higher-income regions. At the same time, less than 20% of adaptation investment needed in these regions is expected to be deployment ready, compared with more than half in higher-income regions, implying a need for innovation in how adaptation is delivered and financed.

Three issues need to be addressed. First, adaptation must become more affordable for households struggling to make ends meet, as about $440 billion in annual adaptation needs could be blocked by competing spending priorities and a lack of creditworthiness. That means cheaper technologies and financing. For example, the municipal authorities in Ahmedabad, India, worked with the Mahila Housing Trust to reduce the cost of heat-reflecting roofs for low-income households through subsidies, credit schemes, and coordinated implementation.

Second, stronger incentives, clearer evidence of benefits, and improved capabilities could unlock about $210 billion in annual adaptation costs. To create more space for rivers to flood safely, the Netherlands’ Room for the River program had to convince some landowners to relinquish their property or change how their land was used, even as the benefits of the program accrued broadly across communities. The program implemented more than 30 projects by aligning incentives through compensation, property purchases, and relocation support, and by coordinating between national and local governments, water authorities, and communities.

Finally, demand exists for the remaining $40 billion in required adaptation measures blocked by barriers, but these projects must be made bankable through innovative revenue mechanisms and financing structures, or with evidence of reliable performance to reduce investor risk. The Drought Tolerant Maize for Africa initiative demonstrates how early-stage funding can help establish a track record for emerging adaptation solutions. Donors supported years of research and field testing, while partnerships with local seed companies helped scale production and distribution. By 2014, drought-tolerant seeds had reached an estimated 5.4 million households.

There are many proven ways to protect people and assets from extreme weather. But advancing adaptation will require each stakeholder to play its part. Companies should integrate climate resilience into investment decisions and develop more affordable adaptation measures. Financial institutions should create financing structures that better capture the economic value of avoided losses. And governments should strengthen incentives, coordinate implementation, and direct scarce public resources toward investments that markets alone cannot deliver.

Adaptation has been shown time and again to deliver substantial economic value. The challenge now is to ensure that those who need to invest have the means—and the incentives—to do so.

Mekala Krishnan is a partner at the McKinsey Global Institute.

Sylvain Johansson is a director at the McKinsey Global Institute.

Kanmani Chockalingam is a senior fellow at the McKinsey Global Institute.

item.title: Put the Ocean at the Center of COP31
item.dc:creator: Peter Thomson
item.description: Last year’s UN Climate Change Conference in Belém, Brazil, put forests high on the climate agenda. This month’s UN Climate Change Conference in Antalya, Turkey, can do the same for the ocean, whose warming threatens not just food and energy security but global survival.
item.content:encoded:
Photo: Orhan Cicek/Anadolu via Getty Images

Last year’s UN Climate Change Conference in Belém, Brazil, put forests high on the climate agenda. This month’s UN Climate Change Conference in Antalya, Turkey, can do the same for the ocean, whose warming threatens not just food and energy security but global survival.

By Peter Thomson

MELBOURNE—For over 30 years, Pacific island countries have issued the same warning at the annual United Nations Climate Change Conference: the warming ocean threatens not just food and energy security, but global survival itself. And almost every year, our warning has been treated as a regional problem, a challenge confined to remote small islands and thus not warranting more than lip service from international leaders.

I wish I could say we were wrong. Instead, the climate devastation unfolding before our eyes, supercharged by an El Niño cycle and record-breaking ocean heat, proves that this crisis does not stop at the shoreline.

Rising sea levels are swallowing fertile farmland, displacing communities, and driving up insurance premiums for families. Ocean warming threatens the energy grids and ports that power the world economy and keep global supply chains running. In the Arctic, 60% of coastal infrastructure, much of which is used for critical security activities, has become vulnerable to erosion. In 2024, the Mediterranean and Black Sea, major fishing and aquaculture hubs that generate $21.5 billion in direct and indirect revenue per year, experienced marine heat waves with temperatures nearly 5° Celsius above normal, raising concerns about food insecurity.

Another overlooked factor is the ocean’s role as the planet’s largest carbon and heat sink, absorbing 30% of CO2 emissions—as much as the world’s forests—and capturing 90% of the excess heat generated by those emissions. But it pays the price: the most heat-sensitive ecosystems are underwater, and every fraction of a degree of global warming beyond the 1.5°C target set by the Paris climate agreement destroys more of them. By 2050, under a 2°C warming scenario, the losses caused by ocean-linked disasters could reach $56 billion, exposing the hard limits of adaptation and the urgent need to keep warming as close to 1.5°C as possible.

These are not trivial problems. They imply major global economic and security risks. And they have existential implications for Pacific island countries: staying below the 1.5°C limit is a matter of survival, which is why we fought so fiercely to secure the Paris climate agreement and, in the intervening years, to stick as closely as possible to that target.

Last year’s UN Climate Change Conference in Belém, Brazil, put forests at the center of the climate agenda. This month’s UN Climate Change Conference (COP31) in Antalya, Turkey, can do the same for the ocean. Political support for ocean-based climate action is strong: more than 100 countries signed a letter declaring that the ocean is a core part of the Paris climate agreement and should be treated as such at COP31.

In practice, this means that negotiators should include the ocean prominently in discussions about reducing emissions, building resilience, and climate finance. Moreover, the latest ocean science must inform the next global stocktake, which would add a level of accountability to climate action by creating ocean-related commitments that countries must report on and standards against which they are measured.

Every country with a coastline should join the Blue NDC Challenge, a group of governments committed to meeting their national climate goals through ocean-based solutions. The ocean can help accelerate the energy transition with the greening of ports and shipping, as well as the development of offshore renewables. Of course, the blue whale in the room is the oil and gas industry. Rapidly shifting away from fossil fuels is the most effective way to reduce the pressure on coral reefs, fisheries, coastal economies, and the local communities that depend on them.

Investment flows must reflect this rising ambition. Current financing for marine protection is estimated at $1.8 billion per year, leaving a gap of approximately $14 billion. And while many proven solutions are ready to scale, coalitions must be mobilized to ensure that marine protected areas can deliver returns through sustainable fishing and tourism revenues.

For too long, the message of Pacific island countries has fallen on deaf ears. COP31 offers a chance to change that. The health of the ocean will shape the future for all people. Now is the time for everyone to accept that it is a shared asset—and a shared responsibility.

Peter Thomson is the United Nations Secretary-General’s Special Envoy for the Ocean.

Originally published on Project Syndicate

item.title: Who's Winning (and Who's Losing) The Ocean?

item.title: The Democrats’ Historic Duty
item.dc:creator: Reed Galen
item.description: While Democrats have good reason to celebrate their historic midterm victory, their current elation must quickly harden into determination. Fortunately, the field for new ideas, systemic and economic, in the US will be the most open it is likely to be for decades.
item.content:encoded:
Photo: Brandon Bell/Getty Images

While Democrats have good reason to celebrate their historic midterm victory, their current elation must quickly harden into determination. Fortunately, the field for new ideas, systemic and economic, in the US will be the most open it is likely to be for decades.

By Reed Galen

WASHINGTON, DC—Twenty years. Thirty years. Eighty years, and even 90. Some of the positions Democratic candidates won in Tuesday’s midterm elections, from Senate seats to attorneys-general, have not had a blue occupant in decades. The outcome of this election, even more than the 2018 midterms, could reshape American politics and policy for years to come. But if the Democrats are to make the most of their gains, they must be ambitious—even audacious.

item.title: Dot-Com Lessons for the AI Bubble
item.dc:creator: Chi Onwurah
item.description: Anyone who lived through the internet boom and bust of the late 1990s and early 2000s should find the current AI investment cycle worryingly familiar. Heavy reliance on debt means that if investors decide to stop lending into the boom, a financial crisis will be inevitable—and far worse than the subprime-mortgage crisis in 2008.
item.content:encoded:
Photo: Lea Suzuki/The San Francisco Chronicle via Getty Images

Anyone who lived through the internet boom and bust of the late 1990s and early 2000s should find the current AI investment cycle worryingly familiar. Heavy reliance on debt means that if investors decide to stop lending into the boom, a financial crisis will be inevitable—and far worse than the subprime-mortgage crisis in 2008.

By Chi Onwurah

LONDON—It is a truth universally acknowledged that transformative new technologies rewrite the rules of finance. Or so we are told in numerous commentaries, social-media posts, and regulatory filings relating to the current AI investment boom, which may well prove to be a bubble.

item.title: China Is Defanging the Dollar, Not Dethroning It
item.dc:creator: Ho-fung Hung
item.description: China offers Iran and Russia a way to circumvent US sanctions and continue doing business. But this comes at an elevated cost, because these countries are paid in onshore, non-convertible renminbi, which they must then convert into dollars using underground financial networks—tacitly reinforcing the greenback’s dominance.
item.content:encoded:
Photo: China Photos/Getty Images

China offers Iran and Russia a way to circumvent US sanctions and continue doing business. But this comes at an elevated cost, because these countries are paid in onshore, non-convertible renminbi, which they must then convert into dollars using underground financial networks—tacitly reinforcing the greenback’s dominance.

By Ho-fung Hung

WASHINGTON, DC—After Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, the United States sought to freeze Russia out of the global financial system, leading many to speculate that weaponization of the US dollar’s dominance of that system would accelerate the world’s shift away from the greenback. Speculation only intensified when the US launched its war against Iran earlier this year and tightened its financial sanctions on the country.

item.title: A Fatal Challenge to Mainstream Economics
item.dc:creator: James K. Galbraith
item.description: The intellectual project on which mainstream economists were raised, and which still forms the backbone of textbook education, has disappeared. What remains is a pastiche of attempted patches, apologies, and corruptions of “heterodox” ideas, all peddled by exponents of an “orthodoxy” that lacks a theoretical core.
item.content:encoded:
Photo: Tim Gidal/Picture Post/Hulton Archive/Getty Images

The intellectual project on which mainstream economists were raised, and which still forms the backbone of textbook education, has disappeared. What remains is a pastiche of attempted patches, apologies, and corruptions of “heterodox” ideas, all peddled by exponents of an “orthodoxy” that lacks a theoretical core.

By James K. Galbraith

KASHGAR—In what is best read as a preemptive swipe at Isabella Weber’s new book, Anti-Fascist Economics, Jason Furman, the chair of the White House Council of Economic Advisers during US President Barack Obama’s second term, recently offered the following half-truth: “the fatal challenge to heterodox economics is that there isn’t actually orthodox economics.”

item.title: The ECB Must Bail Out France
item.dc:creator: Desmond Lachman
item.description: If France is to avoid default, the European Central Bank will need to buy large amounts of its government’s bonds through the Transmission Protection Instrument. But meeting this need—and preventing a potentially disastrous eurozone sovereign-debt-crisis—will require the ECB to waive its own rules.
item.content:encoded:
Photo: Thomas Kienzle/Pool/AFP via Getty Images

If France is to avoid default, the European Central Bank will need to buy large amounts of its government’s bonds through the Transmission Protection Instrument. But meeting this need—and preventing a potentially disastrous eurozone sovereign-debt-crisis—will require the ECB to waive its own rules.

By Desmond Lachman

WASHINGTON, DC—The grandiose claim that “Britannia rules the waves” inspired the wry quip that, in fact, Britannia waives the rules. While the pun was meant as a putdown, waiving rules can be a prudent decision. That is certainly the case for the European Central Bank today, as it weighs its options for helping France, Europe’s second-largest economy, cope with its $4 trillion debt.

item.title: The Rise and Fall of Privacy
item.dc:creator: Tiffany Jenkins
item.description: Privacy is not a natural phenomenon, but rather a historical achievement. It emerged after the Reformation and the wars of religion that followed, reached a high point during the Victorian era, and has now been eroding for decades, long before the advent of the digital economy, social media, and AI.
item.content:encoded:
Photo: Sebastian Kahnert/Picture Alliance via Getty Images

Privacy is not a natural phenomenon, but rather a historical achievement. It emerged after the Reformation and the wars of religion that followed, reached a high point during the Victorian era, and has now been eroding for decades, long before the advent of the digital economy, social media, and AI.

By Tiffany Jenkins

LONDON—In the 17th century, a common injunction held that you should “do nothing privately that you would not do publicly. Task yourself, lest privacy becomes your enemy.” Going further, one preacher even warned that privacy was for “adulterers and murderers.” The devil comes to you when you are on your own. You should find it reassuring to be watched.

Continues on Project Syndicate (subscriber article)

item.title: Good Institutions Require Good People
item.dc:creator: Deirdre Nansen McCloskey
item.description: Well-designed laws, courts, catechisms, extrinsic motives, social approval, and even a few good and decent people are of no avail if too many people do not behave like self-respecting and other-respecting adults. Childish pride and envy, grabbing more of the sweets, Donald Trump-style, do not make for a good society.
item.content:encoded:
Photo: Ryan Murphy/AFP via Getty Images

Well-designed laws, courts, catechisms, extrinsic motives, social approval, and even a few good and decent people are of no avail if too many people do not behave like self-respecting and other-respecting adults. Childish pride and envy, grabbing more of the sweets, Donald Trump-style, do not make for a good society.

By Deirdre Nansen McCloskey

WASHINGTON, DC—We should have learned by now that good politics depends not so much on good institutions as on the moral sentiments supporting them. If bad or unwise people take over your country by coup or by vote, you can’t rely on your institutions to save you. “Add institutions and stir” has never been a consistent recipe for success; good and wise people are.

item.title: Oligarchic World Order
item.dc:creator: David Lingelbach and Valentina Rodríguez Guerra
item.description: Today, some 64 heads of state or government are oligarchs, leading countries that together account for some 60% of global GDP. The question is thus no longer whether oligarchs will rule the world, but rather what kind of world they are building.
item.content:encoded:
Photo: Ricky Carioti/POOL/AFP via Getty Images

Today, some 64 heads of state or government are oligarchs, leading countries that together account for some 60% of global GDP. The question is thus no longer whether oligarchs will rule the world, but rather what kind of world they are building.

By David Lingelbach and Valentina Rodríguez Guerra

BALTIMORE/BOGOTÁ—For most people, the word “oligarch” conjures images of Russian elites who amassed huge fortunes in the wake of the Soviet Union’s collapse or, more recently, the tech billionaires who filled the front row at US President Donald Trump’s second inauguration. But oligarchs are global, systemic, and increasingly entrenched. They are a defining feature of the emerging world order.

item.title: Poland’s Constitutional Civil War
item.dc:creator: Sławomir Sierakowski
item.description: Polish right-wing populists recently stormed the country's Constitutional Tribunal, winning applause from the Kremlin and far-right fellow-travelers across Europe. As in other countries, the constitutional tribunal is the institution that distinguishes a proper democracy from a dictatorship making it a target for authoritarians.
item.content:encoded:
Photo: Getty Images

Polish right-wing populists recently stormed the country's Constitutional Tribunal, winning applause from the Kremlin and far-right fellow-travelers across Europe. As in other countries, the constitutional tribunal is the institution that distinguishes a proper democracy from a dictatorship making it a target for authoritarians.

By Sławomir Sierakowski

WARSAW—In a shocking moment that went viral, Polish President Karol Nawrocki and his cronies were recently filmed breaking into the Constitutional Tribunal in the dead of night and brutally shoving aside the judges they encountered, including an elderly woman. What or who were they coming for?

item.title: The Tech Brotherhood Wants Sovereignty
item.dc:creator: Katharina Pistor
item.description: After centuries of nation-states, a new form of sovereignty is asserting itself. The small fraternity that controls the major digital platforms has already proven capable of even more intrusive and insidious forms of control than most states can muster.
item.content:encoded:
Photo: Getty Images

After centuries of nation-states, a new form of sovereignty is asserting itself. The small fraternity that controls the major digital platforms has already proven capable of even more intrusive and insidious forms of control than most states can muster.

By Katharina Pistor

NEW YORK—Over several centuries, nation-states have come to define the international system and govern much of humanity. After emerging in modern Europe and spreading through colonialism, they eventually made it to every corner of the world through postwar decolonization. Their defining feature is control over territory and its inhabitants, without interference by others.

item.title: The Far Right’s Vision for Europe
item.dc:creator: Mark Leonard
item.description: In many ways, Europe’s far right has already won, regardless of what happens at the ballot box in the coming months. Its parties may still quarrel among themselves, but they agree on the three big issues that will define much of the European political agenda for years to come.
item.content:encoded:
Photo: Romain Perrocheau/AFP via Getty Images

In many ways, Europe’s far right has already won, regardless of what happens at the ballot box in the coming months. Its parties may still quarrel among themselves, but they agree on the three big issues that will define much of the European political agenda for years to come.

By Mark Leonard

BERLIN—Recent events have cast European politics into sharper relief. With left-wing protests, some violent, engulfing cities from Paris to Milan to Madrid, the right has remained focused on big upcoming elections, and most mainstream parties appeared to be in retreat. It may be too soon to guess at the outcomes in Spain, France, Poland, and Italy, but there can be little doubt that far-right and populist ideas will shape the Europe that emerges from these contests. That much is clear to me after spending the past few months talking to leading “new right” politicians and strategists in France, Poland, Germany, and Italy.

item.title: Europe’s Bright Future
item.dc:creator: Thomas Buberl
item.description: A narrative of European decline has taken hold, and if the EU continues on its current path, it may well materialize. But this is not a foregone conclusion: Europe retains considerable strengths on which it can build as it pursues critical reforms aimed at unleashing innovation.
item.content:encoded:
Photo: Daniel Gnap/NurPhoto via Getty Images

A narrative of European decline has taken hold, and if the EU continues on its current path, it may well materialize. But this is not a foregone conclusion: Europe retains considerable strengths on which it can build as it pursues critical reforms aimed at unleashing innovation.

By Thomas Buberl

PARIS—I was born in Germany, I studied in Switzerland and the United Kingdom, and I served as a reserve officer in the French Navy. Today, I am a French citizen leading a French company that operates in more than 50 countries. I am, above all, a European.

item.title: A Debtors’ Club for a Fragmented World
item.dc:creator: Ishac Diwan
item.description: The newly created Borrowers’ Platform aims to facilitate knowledge-sharing and capacity-building among debtor countries, while amplifying their voices in global financial circles. But at a time when the Paris Club of sovereign creditors is increasingly unable to act collectively, the Borrowers’ Platform should ramp up its ambition.
item.content:encoded:
Photo: Subaas Shrestha/NurPhoto via Getty Images

The newly created Borrowers’ Platform aims to facilitate knowledge-sharing and capacity-building among debtor countries, while amplifying their voices in global financial circles. But at a time when the Paris Club of sovereign creditors is increasingly unable to act collectively, the Borrowers’ Platform should ramp up its ambition.

By Ishac Diwan

BANGKOK—For seven decades, some of the world’s biggest official creditors have coordinated their positions in negotiations with debtor countries struggling with repayment. The Paris Club has sought not only to tackle debt treatment for individual sovereigns, but also to shape the rules governing bailouts and conditionality, largely by leveraging its 22 permanent members’ influence at the International Monetary Fund. Now, the world’s debtors have created a club of their own. The question is whether its stated goals are sufficiently ambitious.

item.title: Trump’s Tariff Fiasco Could Save Free Trade
item.dc:creator: Anne O. Krueger
item.description: US President Donald Trump’s tariffs have raised prices and hurt businesses without reducing the trade deficit or creating manufacturing jobs. But global trade has held up better than expected, and growing public opposition to tariffs could pave the way for a retreat from protectionism.
item.content:encoded:
Photo: Allen J. Schaben/Los Angeles Times via Getty Images

US President Donald Trump’s tariffs have raised prices and hurt businesses without reducing the trade deficit or creating manufacturing jobs. But global trade has held up better than expected, and growing public opposition to tariffs could pave the way for a retreat from protectionism.

By Anne O. Krueger

WASHINGTON, DC—In the nearly two years since he returned to the White House, US President Donald Trump has picked up where he left off in his first term, shredding the open multilateral trading system that has served the world so well since the end of World War II. He has imposed sweeping tariffs on dozens of countries, repeatedly raising and lowering them and changing rates on individual goods and countries, seemingly on a whim. As a result, US tariff rates are now higher than at any time since the Great Depression’s Smoot-Hawley tariffs.

Continues on Project Syndicate (registration required)

item.title: If AI Thinks for Us, Democracy Will Suffer
item.dc:creator: John Palfrey
item.description: Whereas the internet buried us in information, AI enables us to outsource analysis altogether. But when it comes to grappling with humanity’s most important questions, we must resist the temptation and recognize that we all have a duty—to each other and to ourselves—to keep “showing up.”
item.content:encoded:
Photo: Patrick Pleul/Picture Alliance via Getty Images

Whereas the internet buried us in information, AI enables us to outsource analysis altogether. But when it comes to grappling with humanity’s most important questions, we must resist the temptation and recognize that we all have a duty—to each other and to ourselves—to keep “showing up.”

By John Palfrey

CHICAGO—Sometime in the 18th century, the Enlightenment settled a contentious, centuries-old question: Where does knowledge come from? For millennia, many people had pointed to God. But the early modern period brought a new consensus, namely that knowledge comes from human scientists working at the edge of what is known, armed with observation, mathematics, experimentation, and logic.
